paragraphs: Mitya crossed the room in long, quick strides and went straight to the table.

“Gentlemen,” he said, loudly, almost shouting, yet stumbling over every word, “I ... I’m all right! Don’t be afraid!” he exclaimed. “I—nothing’s the matter,” he said, suddenly turning to Grushenka, who had shrunk back in her chair toward Kalganov and was gripping his hand. “I ... I’m staying, too. I’m here till morning. Gentlemen, may I stay with you till morning? Only till morning, one last time, in this very room?”
He put this last question to the fat little man with the pipe, who sat on the sofa. The man took the pipe from his lips with great dignity and said sternly:
“_Panie_, this is a private party. There are other rooms.”
“Why, it’s Dmitri Fyodorovitch! What’s the matter with you?” Kalganov broke in. “Sit down with us. How are you?”
“Delighted to see you, my dear ... my precious fellow. I always thought the world of you.” Mitya answered joyfully and eagerly, and held out his hand across the table at once.
“Ow! What a grip you have! You’ve nearly broken my fingers,” laughed Kalganov.

“He always grips like that, always,” Grushenka put in cheerfully, with a timid smile. One look at Mitya’s face had suddenly convinced her that he wasn’t going to make a scene. She watched him with keen curiosity, and with some worry still. Something in him struck her. In fact, the last thing she had expected was for him to walk in and talk like this at such a moment.
“Good evening,” Maximov said blandly from the left. Mitya rushed over to him, too.

“Good evening. You’re here, too! I’m so glad to find you here, too! Gentlemen, gentlemen, I—” (He turned again to the Polish gentleman with the pipe, plainly taking him for the most important person there.) “I flew here.... I wanted to spend my last day, my last hour in this room, in this very room ... where I, too, worshiped ... my queen.... Forgive me, _panie_,” he cried wildly, “I flew here and swore— Oh, don’t be afraid, it’s my last night! Let’s drink to a good understanding between us. They’ll bring the wine in a minute.... I brought this along.” (Something made him pull out his bundle of notes.) “Allow me, _panie_! I want music, singing, a revel, just as we had before. But the worm, the useless worm, will crawl away, and there’ll be nothing left of him. On my last night I’ll honor my day of joy.”

He was almost choking. He had so much, so much to say, and nothing came out of his mouth but odd exclamations. The Pole stared hard at him, then at the bundle of notes in his hand, then at Grushenka, and plainly didn’t know what to make of it.
“If my suverin lady is permitting—” he started.

“What’s ‘suverin’? ‘Sovereign,’ I suppose?” Grushenka cut in. “You talk so funny I can’t help laughing. Sit down, Mitya, what are you going on about? Please don’t scare us. You won’t scare us, will you? If you won’t, I’m glad to see you ...”
“Me, scare you?” cried Mitya, flinging up his hands. “Oh, pass me by, go your way, I won’t stand in your road!...”

And suddenly he startled them all, and no doubt himself too. He dropped onto a chair and burst into tears, turning his face to the far wall, his arms wrapped tight around the chair back as though he were hugging it.

“Oh, come now, what a man you are!” cried Grushenka reproachfully. “That’s how he always comes to see me—he starts talking, and I can’t make out what he means. He cried like this once before, and here he is crying again! It’s a disgrace! What are you crying for? _As though you had anything to cry for!_” she added mysteriously, stressing every word, a little irritably.
“I ... I’m not crying.... Well, good evening!” He swung round in his chair at once and laughed—not his abrupt, wooden laugh but a long, shaky, silent, nervous one.

“Well, you’re at it again.... Come on, cheer up, cheer up!” Grushenka coaxed him. “I’m very glad you came, very glad, Mitya, do you hear, I’m very glad! I want him to stay here with us,” she declared to the whole room, though her words were clearly aimed at the man on the sofa. “That’s what I want, that’s what I want! And if he goes, I’m going, too!” she added, her eyes flashing.
“Whatever my queen commands is law!” announced the Pole, kissing Grushenka’s hand with a gallant air. “Please, _panie_, join our company,” he added politely to Mitya.
Mitya sprang up, evidently meaning to launch into another tirade, but no words came.
“Let’s drink, _panie_,” was all he blurted out in place of a speech. Everyone laughed.

“Heavens! I thought he was going to start in again!” Grushenka said nervously. “Listen, Mitya,” she went on, pressing him, “stop prancing about. But it’s nice that you’ve brought champagne. I’d like some myself, and I can’t bear liqueurs. And best of all, you’re here yourself. We were dreadfully bored.... Have you come on a spree again, I suppose? But put that money away. Where did you get so much?”

The whole time, Mitya had been holding the crumpled bundle of notes in his hand, and every eye in the room was on it, the Poles’ most of all. Embarrassed, he hastily shoved it into his pocket. He blushed. Just then the innkeeper came in with an uncorked bottle of champagne and glasses on a tray. Mitya grabbed the bottle, but he was so rattled that he had no idea what to do with it. Kalganov took it out of his hands and poured the champagne.

“Another! Bring another bottle!” Mitya shouted to the innkeeper. Forgetting to clink glasses with the Pole he had so solemnly asked to drink to their good understanding, he downed his glass without waiting for anyone else. His whole face changed at once. The solemn, tragic look he had walked in with was gone, and something childlike took its place. He seemed suddenly gentle and subdued. He looked around at everyone, shy and happy, with a constant little nervous laugh, and with the blissful look of a dog that has done wrong, been punished and been forgiven. He seemed to have forgotten everything, and he gazed around at them all with a childlike smile of delight. He looked at Grushenka, laughing the whole time, and pulled his chair right up beside hers. Gradually he had begun to form some idea of the two Poles, though he had no clear picture of them yet.

The Pole on the sofa impressed him with his dignified manner and his Polish accent, and most of all with his pipe. “Well, so what? It’s a good thing he smokes a pipe,” he thought. The Pole’s puffy, middle-aged face, with its tiny nose and its two very thin, pointed, dyed, cheeky-looking mustaches, hadn’t raised the slightest suspicion in Mitya so far. He wasn’t even particularly struck by the man’s ridiculous wig, made in Siberia, with love-locks combed foolishly forward over the temples. “It must be all right, since he wears a wig,” he went on, musing blissfully. The other Pole, the younger one, was staring at the company with insolent defiance and listening to the talk in silent contempt. He impressed Mitya only by his great height, which made a striking contrast with the Pole on the sofa. “If he stood up, he’d be six foot three.” The thought flitted through Mitya’s head. It also occurred to him that this man must be the other’s friend, a kind of “bodyguard,” and that the big Pole was no doubt at the little Pole with the pipe’s service. But all this seemed to Mitya perfectly proper and not to be questioned. In his doglike mood of submission, every feeling of rivalry had died out.

He completely failed to understand Grushenka’s mood, or the mysterious tone of some of her words. All he understood, with a thrill in his heart, was that she was being kind to him, that she had forgiven him and let him sit by her. He was beside himself with joy, watching her sip her champagne. The silence in the room seemed to strike him, though, and he looked around at everyone with expectant eyes.
“Why are we just sitting here, gentlemen? Why don’t you get something going?” his smiling eyes seemed to ask.
“He keeps talking nonsense, and we’ve all been laughing,” Kalganov said suddenly, as if he had read Mitya’s thought, and he pointed at Maximov.
Mitya promptly stared at Kalganov, then at Maximov.
“Talking nonsense, is he?” he laughed his short, wooden laugh, suddenly delighted about something—“ha ha!”
“Yes. Believe it or not, he swears that all our cavalry officers in the twenties married Polish women. Isn’t that awful rot?”
“Polish women?” Mitya repeated, in sheer ecstasy.

Kalganov knew very well how Mitya felt about Grushenka, and he had guessed about the Pole as well. But that interested him little, perhaps not at all. What interested him was Maximov. He had come here with Maximov by chance, and he was meeting the Poles at this inn for the first time in his life. He had known Grushenka before and had once visited her with someone, but she hadn’t warmed to him. Tonight, though, she looked at him very fondly. Before Mitya arrived she had been fussing over him, but somehow it didn’t move him. He was a boy, not yet twenty, dressed like a dandy, with a very charming fair-skinned face and splendid thick fair hair. Out of that fair face looked beautiful pale blue eyes, with an intelligent and at times even deep expression, beyond his years in fact, though the young man sometimes looked and talked just like a child, and wasn’t the least ashamed of it, even when he noticed it himself. As a rule he was very willful, even capricious, though always friendly. Now and then there was something fixed and stubborn in his look. He would look at you and listen, and all the while seem to be dreaming doggedly of something else. He was often listless and lazy; at other times he would get excited, sometimes, it seemed, over the most trivial things.

“Just think, I’ve been dragging him around with me for the last four days,” he went on, drawling lazily, quite naturally though, with no affectation at all. “Ever since your brother, remember, shoved him off the carriage and sent him flying. That’s when I took an interest in him, and I took him with me to the country. But he talks such rot that I’m ashamed to be seen with him. I’m taking him back.”
“The gentleman has not seen Polish ladies, and says what is not possible,” the Pole with the pipe told Maximov.
He spoke Russian reasonably well, better, at any rate, than he let on. Whenever he used a Russian word, he twisted it into a Polish shape.
“But I was married to a Polish lady myself,” Maximov tittered.
“But did you serve in the cavalry? You were talking about the cavalry. Were you a cavalry officer?” Kalganov chimed in immediately.
“A cavalry officer, is he? Ha ha!” cried Mitya, listening eagerly, his questioning eyes going from one speaker to the next, as if there were no telling what he might hear from any of them.

“No, you see,” Maximov said, turning to him. “What I mean is, those pretty Polish ladies ... when they danced the mazurka with our Uhlans ... when one of them dances the mazurka with a Uhlan, she jumps onto his knee like a kitten ... a little white one ... and the _pan_-father and _pan_-mother watch and let it happen.... They let it happen ... and the next day the Uhlan comes and proposes.... That’s how it is ... proposes, he he!” Maximov finished, tittering.

“The _pan_ is a _lajdak_!” the tall Pole on the chair suddenly growled, crossing one leg over the other. Mitya’s eye fell on his huge greased boot with its thick, dirty sole. Both Poles’ clothes looked rather greasy.
“Now what’s this, _lajdak_! What’s he scolding about?” said Grushenka, suddenly annoyed.
“_Pani_ Agrippina, the gentleman saw servant girls in Poland, not ladies of good family,” the Pole with the pipe told Grushenka.
“You can count on that,” the tall Pole snapped scornfully.
“What next! Let him talk! People talk, so why stop them? It livens things up,” Grushenka said crossly.
“I’m not stopping them, _pani_,” said the Pole in the wig. He gave Grushenka a long look, sank back into dignified silence, and went on sucking his pipe.

“No, no. The Polish gentleman told the truth.” Kalganov was worked up again, as though it were a question of enormous importance. “He’s never been to Poland, so how can he talk about it? I suppose you weren’t married in Poland, were you?”

“No, in the Province of Smolensk. But a Uhlan had already brought her to Russia before that, my future wife, together with her mamma, her aunt, and another woman relative who had a grown-up son. He brought her straight from Poland and handed her over to me. He was a lieutenant in our regiment, a very nice young man. At first he meant to marry her himself. In the end he didn’t, because she turned out to be lame.”
“So you married a lame woman?” cried Kalganov.
“Yes. The two of them deceived me a little at the time, and kept it hidden. I thought she was hopping; she kept hopping.... I thought it was for fun.”
“She was so happy to be marrying you!” yelled Kalganov in a ringing, childish voice.

“Yes, so happy. But it turned out to be for quite another reason. Later, once we were married, that very evening after the wedding, she confessed, and asked forgiveness in a very touching way. ‘As a child I jumped over a puddle once,’ she said, ‘and hurt my leg.’ He he!”
Kalganov burst into the most childish laughter and nearly fell onto the sofa. Grushenka laughed, too. Mitya was at the peak of happiness.

“You know, that’s the truth, he isn’t lying this time,” Kalganov exclaimed, turning to Mitya; “and you know, he’s been married twice; it’s his first wife he’s talking about. But his second wife, you know, ran away, and she’s alive now.”
“Is that possible?” said Mitya, turning quickly to Maximov, utterly astonished.

“Yes. She did run away. I’ve had that unpleasant experience,” Maximov agreed modestly, “with a _monsieur_. And what made it worse, she’d had all my little property made over to her beforehand. ‘You’re an educated man,’ she told me. ‘You can always make a living.’ With that she settled my affairs. A venerable bishop once said to me: ‘One of your wives was lame, but the other was too light-footed.’ He he!”

“Listen, listen!” cried Kalganov, bubbling over. “If he tells lies—and he often does—he only does it to amuse us all. There’s no harm in that, is there? You know, sometimes I like him. He’s dreadfully low, but it comes naturally to him, eh? Don’t you think so? Some people are low for gain, but he’s simply made that way. Just think, he claims (he argued about it all the way yesterday) that Gogol wrote _Dead Souls_ about him. Remember, there’s a landowner named Maximov in it, the one Nozdryov thrashed. He was charged, remember, ‘with inflicting bodily injury with rods on the landowner Maximov while drunk.’ Can you believe it, he claims he was that Maximov and that he was beaten! Now can that be true? Tchitchikov made his journey at the very latest at the beginning of the twenties, so the dates don’t fit. He couldn’t have been thrashed then, could he?”
It was hard to guess what Kalganov was so stirred up about, but his excitement was real. Mitya went along with him without protest.
“Well, so what if they did thrash him!” he cried, laughing.
“It isn’t that they thrashed me, exactly, but what I mean is—” Maximov put in.
“What do you mean? Either they thrashed you or they didn’t.”
“What o’clock is it, _panie_?” the Pole with the pipe asked his tall friend, looking bored. The other shrugged in answer. Neither of them had a watch.

“Why not talk? Let other people talk. Are other people not allowed to talk just because you’re bored?” Grushenka flew at him, obviously set on picking a quarrel. Something seemed to dawn on Mitya’s mind for the first time. This time the Pole answered with unmistakable irritation.
“_Pani_, I raised no objection. I said nothing.”
“Fine, then. Come, tell us your story,” Grushenka called to Maximov. “Why is everyone so quiet?”

“There’s nothing to tell, it’s all so silly,” Maximov answered at once, plainly pleased, with a little mincing air. “Besides, it’s all allegory in Gogol, because he gave every name a meaning. Nozdryov was really called Nosov, and Kuvshinikov had quite a different name, Shkvornev. Fenardi really was called Fenardi, only he wasn’t an Italian but a Russian. And Mamsel Fenardi was a pretty girl, with her pretty little legs in tights and a short little skirt with spangles, and she kept turning round and round, only not for four hours but for four minutes, and she bewitched everyone...”
“But what did they beat you for?” cried Kalganov.
“For Piron!” Maximov answered.
“What Piron?” cried Mitya.

“The famous French writer Piron. We were all drinking, a big party of us, in a tavern at that same fair. They had invited me, and first of all I started quoting epigrams. ‘Is that you, Boileau? What a funny outfit!’ and Boileau replies that he’s off to a masquerade, meaning the baths, he he! They took it as aimed at them, so I hurried to recite another, a very biting one, known to every educated person:
Yes, Sappho and Phaon are we! But one grief is weighing on me. You don’t know your way to the sea!

That offended them even more, and they began to abuse me in the most unseemly way. And as bad luck would have it, to smooth things over I started telling a very cultured anecdote about Piron, how he was refused entry to the French Academy and, to get his revenge, wrote his own epitaph:
Ci-gît Piron qui ne fut rien, Pas même académicien.
They grabbed me and thrashed me.”
“But what for? What for?”
“For my education. A man can be thrashed for anything,” Maximov concluded, briefly and sententiously.
